title: Trump Shifts Midterm Campaign to Deep‑Red States, Skipping Expected Battlegrounds
body:
President Donald Trump announced a plan to hit the campaign trail in 35 of the nation’s most competitive House and Senate contests as the midterm election season accelerates, but his first stops this October will be in Alabama and Oklahoma—states that are solidly Republican and far from the battlegrounds he promised to target.

The former president’s itinerary, unveiled during a rally in Montgomery, Ala., listed a slate of swing districts across the Midwest, the South and the West where Republicans are fighting narrow leads against Democratic challengers. Yet the opening leg of his road tour will see him addressing audiences in two deep‑red states, a move that has drawn criticism from GOP strategists and raised questions about the timing and focus of his outreach.

Trump’s decision to start in Alabama and Oklahoma reflects a broader pattern of his post‑presidential political activity. Since leaving the White House, he has cultivated a loyal base through high‑profile rallies, fundraising drives and frequent media appearances. By kicking off the campaign in his party’s strongholds, Trump can guarantee enthusiastic crowds, large donations and a media‑friendly environment that reinforces his narrative of a “war on the Republic.” Analysts note that the early rallies also serve as a testing ground for new messaging and campaign staff ahead of the more contentious swing‑state visits later in the month.

Critics within the Republican establishment argue that the timing is counterproductive. “If Trump truly wants to influence the 35 battleground races he highlighted, he should be on the ground in places like Pennsylvania’s 7th district, Arizona’s 2nd, or Georgia’s 6th as soon as possible,” said political consultant Maria Delgado, who has worked on several GOP congressional campaigns. “Starting in states where the outcome is a foregone conclusion does little to shift the dynamics in those tight contests and may even signal a lack of urgency.”

Supporters, however, contend that the early rallies are a strategic move to shore up the party’s base before the crucial swing‑state push. By energizing voters in Alabama and Oklahoma, Trump hopes to boost turnout in down‑ballot races that could affect the overall composition of Congress, such as the Senate seats held by Republicans in both states. Moreover, the rallies provide a platform to launch new policy proposals and attack Democratic incumbents, setting the tone for the upcoming weeks.

The broader context of the 2024 midterms adds layers of complexity to Trump’s campaign calculus. Republicans are currently defending a narrow majority in the House and a slim edge in the Senate, with many analysts warning that the party’s fortunes hinge on a handful of districts that swung in 2022. Meanwhile, the Democratic Party is banking on a coordinated national strategy that emphasizes local issues and candidate quality, aiming to offset any boost the former president might give to GOP candidates.

As the October calendar unfolds, Trump is expected to pivot toward the promised battlegrounds, with planned appearances in Michigan, Wisconsin, Nevada and New Hampshire slated for later in the month. Whether his early forays into Alabama and Oklahoma will translate into tangible gains in the competitive races remains to be seen, but the move underscores his continued influence over the Republican agenda and the high stakes of the upcoming midterm elections.

Looking ahead, the effectiveness of Trump’s campaign strategy will likely be measured not just by the size of the crowds he draws, but by the impact on voter turnout and candidate performance in the 35 targeted contests. With just weeks left before Election Day, both parties will be watching closely to see if the former president’s rallying tour can tip the balance in the closely watched races that will determine the direction of Congress for the next two years.
